feedback: If a learner treats one grouping as the 'real' one, show two valid groupings of the same set side by side using criteria they actually applied (e.g. by body covering; by diet) and ask which rule each pile follows — both are legitimate.
If a learner says the animal 'changed' when it moved piles, point back to the single organism and ask: 'What about the frog is different now? Or did only our rule change?'
If a learner sorts sensibly but cannot name the rule, ask 'What is the same about everything in this pile?' to surface the criterion already in use — scaffold, don't reteach.
If a learner sorts by colour or size, contrast that with fur/backbone and ask which features tell you more about the animals themselves.
activities.intendedInsight: Groups are not fixed labels stuck to each creature; a group is a tool we impose by choosing a criterion. The same organism belongs to different groups depending on the feature we sort by.
learnerActions: Take a tray of 8–12 familiar organisms (pictured or on cards) and sort them into groups under one chosen rule, e.g. body covering: fur / feathers / scales / bare skin.
State out loud or write the rule you are grouping by before you start each sort.

Now change the criterion to 'what it eats', then to 'how many legs', then to 'lives in water or not', and re-sort the SAME animals each time; watch which animals leave one pile and join a different one.

Track one organism across the sorts you actually perform, e.g. a frog: under the body-covering sort it sits in the 'bare skin' pile, but under a 'lives in or near water' habitat sort it joins the fish (many adult frogs also spend time on land, so agree the rule's wording first) — note that the frog itself did not change, only the rule did.
As an extension, try a two-way (Carroll or Venn) sort that crosses two criteria at once, e.g. 'has wings' against 'lays eggs', and notice that where one organism lands depends on both rules together.
In a 'make your own group' mode, invent your own rule, sort by it, and check that every animal in a pile really shares that feature (test your rule for consistency).
activities.title: Multi-criteria sorting bench: group the same set two ways

feedback: If a learner sorts a bat with birds because it flies, contrast flight (shared by unrelated animals) with fur/milk, and ask which features a bat shares with a dog that a robin does not.
If a learner insists each animal has one correct box, show the bat in both 'can fly' (with robin, butterfly) and 'feeds its young milk' (with dog, whale) and point out both sorts are valid.

If a learner concludes a whale 'is a fish', clarify that grouping it with fish only reflects the 'lives in water'/shape criterion, while breathing air and feeding its young milk group it with mammals and reflect how the animals are really related.
If a learner can't say why a placement is right, ask 'What rule did you use to decide?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to place organisms correctly AND name the criterion, and to show one organism fits two groups, demonstrates that grouping depends on the chosen feature rather than a single hidden truth; some features (feeds milk) also reflect how animals are actually related.
learnerActions: Place given organisms into vertebrates/invertebrates (or another named pair), then state the criterion that pair uses.
Use a two-way (Carroll/Venn) grid for a single criterion pair, e.g. 'has wings' and 'lays eggs', and explain why a chosen animal lands in its cell.

Answer: 'Does a whale go with the fish or with the dog? What does it depend on?' and explain your reasoning — grouping a whale with fish reflects only a 'lives in water'/body-shape criterion, while grouping it with the dog reflects 'breathes air / feeds its young milk', so the answer depends on the rule you choose.
Place the SAME animal into two different correct groups under two different criteria and say why each placement is right.
Discuss: 'Is there a wrong way to group these animals, or just different ways?' and 'Which grouping tells you more about how the animals are really related — can fly or feeds milk? Why?'
activities.title: Check and defend: place, justify, and relate groupings
